title: Jagannath rides out
hookLine: a carver's closed door, a god left unfinished, and the lord of the world who leaves his temple once a year for everyone
carry: the lord of the world comes out to everyone
tomorrow: who counts as family? an old line answers in two words.
last: DO THE WORK. OFFER IT TO KRISHNA.

lines: UNFINISHED. WORSHIP THEM AS THEY ARE.
cards: As Puri tells it, King Indradyumna is shown in a dream that a holy log will wash up on the shore. It does.

But no carver can cut it, until an old craftsman appears and says he'll make the images, on one condition: lock him in, and no one opens the door until he's done. Days pass behind the door, with the sound of carving.
Then the sound stops. The queen fears the old man has died, and the king opens the door early. The carver is gone.
The images stand there unfinished, with no hands and no feet. And the king is told in a dream: worship them just as they are.

teach.b: That's how Jagannath of Puri came to look the way he does: round eyes, a wooden face, short arms. His name has a join in it.

Jagat, the world, plus natha, lord. Before the n, the t got ready and turned into an n too: Jagannath, lord of the world. Most days he's inside the great temple at Puri, and not everyone may enter it.
Even so, there's an image of him at the Lion Gate called Patitapavana, savior of the fallen, for those who can't go in.

But once a year, at Rath Yatra, he comes out. Jagannath, his brother Balabhadra and his sister Subhadra are carried out and ride huge wooden chariots down the Grand Road, to the Gundicha temple, and stay about a week.
Anyone at all can see him in the street, and that seeing has a name: darshan, to see God and be seen by him.
Devotees say even one glimpse of him on the chariot is a blessing, and anyone can take hold of the ropes and pull.

teach.h: THE LORD OF THE WORLD COMES OUT TO EVERYONE.
teach.b: Before the chariots roll, the king of Puri sweeps the chariot floor with a golden broom, a king cleaning for the lord of the world. The teaching: God doesn't wait only behind temple walls for the right people.
Once a year, he comes out to all of them, unfinished hands and all.

how: At Rath Yatra in Puri, Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra ride three chariots to the Gundicha temple and anyone may pull the ropes; the king of Puri sweeps the chariots first. Rath Yatras are now also held in cities around the world.

games.q: the lord of the world — tap the pairs.
p: the king who opened the door too early
the chariot festival: he comes out to the street

s: at Rath Yatra, only priests may pull Jagannath's chariot
anyone can take hold of the ropes and have darshan. that's the point: he comes out to everyone.
in Puri's story, the images were left unfinished when the door opened early
and the king was told to worship them as they are.
Jagannath has no trace of jagat, the world, in it
the t became n before natha. the world is still there.

games.q: a friend asks why a god would leave his temple and ride through crowded streets. what does Rath Yatra teach?
o: the lord of the world comes out so everyone, inside or outside the temple, can see him and pull the rope.
the temple needs cleaning, so the images are moved out of the way.
it's a parade for tourists; the real worship is only inside.
games.why: Jagannath means lord of the world. once a year he leaves the temple, and anyone at all may see him and take the rope. even the king sweeps the chariot first.

practice: Picture the Grand Road: the crowd, the drums, three chariots, ropes thick as an arm. Picture taking hold of a rope beside a stranger. If you pray, say softly, Jai Jagannath.
If you don't, think of one person who usually stays outside the room you're in, and one small way to bring them in this week. Then let the picture go, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Sandhi plainly: today, a t that gets ready for the n beside it. The world is still inside Jagannath.

orig.note: Sanskrit: jagannātha, lord of the world; jagat + nātha, the t turned into n before the n.

carryVoice: Your line: the lord of the world comes out to everyone. Unfinished hands, and a rope for anyone. Rest easy.

sources.ref: The Indradyumna legend of Jagannath (the log from the sea, the carver behind closed doors, the images left unfinished): Purushottama Kshetra Mahatmya (Skanda Purana) and Odia tellings, which vary in detail

Rath Yatra at Puri (three chariots to the Gundicha temple; the ropes; darshan of the deities on the chariots; chhera pahara, the king sweeping the chariots); the Patitapavana image at the Lion Gate (Singhadwara)
Ashtadhyayi 8.4.45 (a stop before a nasal may become nasal): jagannātha (jagat + nātha)
